name: Angelo Mozilo

summary.text: Angelo Mozilo was chief executive of Countrywide Financial, the mortgage lender acquired by Bank of America in 2008. On June 4, 2009 the SEC charged Mozilo, former president David Sambol and former CFO Eric Sieracki with securities fraud, alleging they misled investors about Countrywide's credit risk, and charged Mozilo with insider trading for selling shares worth more than $139 million under 10b5-1 plans set up in late 2006. On October 15, 2010 Mozilo settled, agreeing to a $22.5 million penalty, which the SEC called the largest ever against a senior executive of a public company, plus $45 million in disgorgement and a permanent bar from serving as an officer or director of a public company. House Oversight Committee reports describe a Countrywide 'VIP' loan program in which Mozilo personally authorized exceptions for influential borrowers.

facts.claim: On June 4, 2009 the SEC charged Mozilo, former Countrywide president David Sambol and former CFO Eric Sieracki with securities fraud, alleging they misled investors as the subprime mortgage crisis emerged; the complaint alleged Mozilo set up four 10b5-1 sales plans in October, November and December 2006 while aware of material non-public information about Countrywide's increasing credit risk and sold shares between November 2006 and October 2007 for more than $139 million.
facts.quote: The SEC alleged that Mozilo engaged in insider trading by establishing four 10b5-1 sales plans in October, November, and December 2006 while aware of material, non-public information about Countrywide's increasing credit risk.

sources.title: Litigation Release No. 21068A: SEC v. Angelo Mozilo, David Sambol, and Eric Sieracki
Former Countrywide CEO Angelo Mozilo to Pay SEC's Largest-Ever Financial Penalty Against a Public Company's Senior Executive

facts.claim: On October 15, 2010 Mozilo agreed to pay a $22.5 million penalty to settle the SEC's charges, which the SEC said was the largest penalty ever paid by a senior executive of a public company, plus $45 million in disgorgement, for a total of $67.5 million to be returned to harmed investors.
facts.quote: Mozilo also agreed to $45 million in disgorgement of ill-gotten gains to settle the SEC's disclosure violation and insider trading charges against him, for a total financial settlement of $67.5 million that will be returned to harmed investors.

facts.claim: The settlement permanently bars Mozilo from serving as an officer or director of a publicly traded company.
facts.quote: It permanently bars Mozilo from ever again serving as an officer or director of a publicly traded company.

facts.claim: In the same settlement Sambol agreed to repay $5 million in profits and pay $520,000 in civil penalties, and Sieracki agreed to pay $130,000 in civil penalties.
facts.quote: Sambol agreed to repay $5 million in profits and pay $520,000 in civil penalties, and Sieracki agreed to pay $130,000 in civil penalties.

facts.claim: SEC distribution records show Mozilo received a $25 million credit toward his settlement for sums credited to him in the securities class action In re Countrywide Financial Corporation Securities Litigation.
facts.quote: Mozilo received a credit of $25,000,000 for sums credited to him as part of his settlement in the securities class action In re Countrywide Financial Corporation Securities Litigation.

facts.claim: A 2009 House Oversight Committee Republican staff report, 'Friends of Angelo', describes a Countrywide VIP loan program offering preferential treatment to potentially influential borrowers to build goodwill in Washington, in which VIP borrowers were told Mozilo priced their loans personally and Mozilo personally authorized overrides when VIP loans broke company policy.
facts.quote: Mozilo was notified and would personally authorize overrides

facts.claim: NPR reported in June 2008 that Portfolio magazine cited Countrywide e-mails listing Senators Christopher Dodd and Kent Conrad as 'friends of Angelo'; both senators said they did not expect special treatment. CNN reported in 2012 that Bank of America discontinued the VIP program when it acquired Countrywide in 2008.
facts.quote: Portfolio magazine cites corporate e-mails that listed both senators as "friends of Angelo."

openQuestions: Site claim that Countrywide under Mozilo was part of a 'subprime fraud conveyor' with 'systematic fabrication of W-2s' and 'NINJA' loans: the SEC case concerned disclosure to investors and insider trading, not loan-file fabrication; no source returned supports the W-2 claim.

Site claim that criminal securitization 'carries zero executive jail time': consistent with the record found for Mozilo, who faced civil SEC charges only; no criminal charge against him was found in the sources returned.
Bank of America's 2008 acquisition of Countrywide is referenced by CNN but the deal date and terms were not retrieved; the FCIC report's treatment of Countrywide was not retrieved.
